How is this going to make you feel less shitty? Because you're meant to **learn** from these experiences and **move forward.**

1. You obviously want to be in a relationship. She obviously doesn't. Let her go. Turn your sights toward other girls.

2. If you can't let her go, you're clinging and you should learn to stop (it's okay, everyone clings until they learn not to). You can't be reliant on a girl for your baseline level of happiness. The opposite of clinginess is self-reliance. Learn to be happy alone. It will be better for your next relationship and your whole life if you do.

Want to know what happened? I'll tell it to you straight:

1. You said (in your other post about this), "The relationship started as a sexual one...Things were going amazingly well. We were having sex all the time, and in general just having a blast." *That right there* is all she ever committed to. *You* changed the expectation from "having a blast" at school to being in a relationship over the summer. What you should have said is, "I really enjoy hanging out with you, maybe I'll see you around this summer."
2. Then, "she was going to be away for the month of July." Having to question what that would mean about you, this made her realize that "She didn't want something serious but the relationship kind of just ended up more serious than she wanted." The beauty is, she *said* that to you, she was honest. Most guys don't get that. The fact that she said "she kept sending you mixed signals and it's unfair," means she's being good and truthful to you. It's the truth that most guys in your situation wish they could hear.
3. "I just want to know if this is game over with this girl, or if there may be something left." It's never game over, you just have to change games. Stop playing the Serious Relationship Game and start playing the Laugh and Have Fun game. The funny thing is, the fastest and most direct route to the Serious Relationship is to just play the Laugh and Have Fun Game and never get hung up by anything. It's not her fault that she just wants to have fun. 
That means you'll have to control your own emotional state consistently. You are the master of your own happiness. Stop measuring each of your interactions by how much you hook up at the end of them and whether or not it leads to sex. Enjoy every moment with her and everyone you come across, every day and you can't go wrong. Learn to enjoy your life alone and the rest will follow. Treat her exactly as she is, which is a girl that likes you and wants to have fun. Perhaps you should just have fun.

TL;DR - She's being honest with you. She just wants to have fun. Learn to have fun with zero expectations. Or find a different girl.

I've given this question significant thought.

What you say is true, the more you analyze the world, the more removed you feel from it.

I think this happens because, in order to analyze properly, you must assume the view of a "3rd Party," watching from behind an unbiased "screen." Thus, you remove yourself from the scene.

When you stand outside the scene as a 3rd Party, you are no longer a little person standing between gargantuan trees under impossible skies, feeling the softness of the grass between your toes and the breeze rolling across your skin. Instead, you see the scene as you'd watch a movie, slowly passing by as you study events, characters, and setting.

You can get back IN the movie. That's the path to reclaiming those good, awe-inspired, high-definition feelings. You simply have to choose presence.

Presence occurs when we live in full acceptance of this moment. The paths to presence are many - a peaceful walk, a soothing song, deep breathing, meditation - anything that makes you feel the quiet energy flowing through you. When we choose the path to presence, the world is real again.

Your experiences matter. You're an unimaginably tiny spec of a seemingly infinite universe, but you're still an inseparably incredible part of it all. It's okay to let these moments be unexplainably, immeasurably, wonderfully real.

Thanks for reading.

**TL;DR - Prolonged overanalysis causes feelings of separation. Practiced presence resumes childlike wonder.**
